details:
**Zamzam**
The sacred well in Mecca that miraculously sprang up when an angel (Gabriel) struck the ground with his heel or wing to save Hagar (Hajar) and her infant son Ishmael. Pilgrims drink its water, and in 930 CE the Qarmatians desecrated it by throwing corpses into it when they sacked Mecca.

**Safa and Marwa**
The two hills in Mecca between which Hagar ran seven times searching for water for Ishmael. Pilgrims re-enact her search by walking between them seven times during the Hajj and Umrah, a rite called the sa'i.

**Wudu and ghusl**
Wudu is the Islamic ritual washing of the face, hands, arms, head, and feet with water before salat (prayer). Ghusl is the full-body ablution required after major impurities such as sexual intercourse, menstruation, or childbirth.

**Tayammum**
The Islamic dry ablution performed with clean sand, earth, or dust when water is unavailable or unsafe to use. It serves the same purpose as wudu.

**Baptism**
The Christian sacrament of initiation in which water is used to wash away sin, performed by full immersion, by affusion (pouring), or by aspersion (sprinkling). A baptism that includes naming an infant is often called a christening, and the Holy Spirit is often compared to the "water of life."

**Holy water**
Water blessed by a priest, often with exorcised salt added in the form of a cross, and used to bless people, homes, and cars. Congregants dip their fingers in it from a stoup or font when entering a church to make the sign of the cross, and it is sprinkled with an aspergillum, which replaced the earlier hyssop branch.

**Mikveh**
The Jewish ritual bath used for purification, for example by women after menstruation or childbirth and by converts. Water is also used in taharah, the ritual washing of a body before burial, and in netilat yadayim, the ritual washing of the hands before eating bread.

**Wedding at Cana**
The Gospel of John's account of Jesus's first miracle, in which he turned water into wine at a wedding feast after telling his mother, "My hour has not yet come." Jesus also famously walked on water during a storm on the Sea of Galilee, where Peter at first thought he was a ghost.

**Ganges River and the Kumbh Mela**
The Ganges (Ganga) is Hinduism's holiest river, personified as the goddess Ganga, and bathing in it is believed to wash away sins. The Kumbh Mela is a massive pilgrimage festival at which millions of Hindus bathe in sacred rivers such as the Ganges, and devotees at Varanasi bathe from the steps called ghats.

**Every living thing created from water**
A teaching of the Quran, found in Surah 21, verse 30 and Surah 24, verse 45, that God made every living creature from water. The second verse goes on to distinguish creatures that crawl on their bellies from those that walk on two or four legs.

**Water as the best charity**
A hadith in which Muhammad, asked by Sa'd ibn Ubadah what the best form of charity was, answered "water," after which Sa'd dug a well. Islamic jurisprudence (fiqh) also classifies water into mutlaq (pure, unmixed) and mudaf (mixed) types for purification purposes.

**Misogi and harae**
Shinto purification rituals. Misogi is purification by washing the body in water, often under a waterfall or in the sea, while harae is the broader rite of purification that can use water and salt to remove impurity.

**Moses striking the rock**
The episode in which Moses brought forth water for the thirsty Israelites by striking a rock with his staff. In the Book of Numbers, he was punished by being barred from the Promised Land for striking the rock twice instead of speaking to it as God commanded.

**Epiphany (Theophany) and Timkat**
Eastern Christian feasts commemorating Jesus's baptism in the Jordan, marked by the Great Blessing of the Waters, as opposed to the "lesser" blessing that can be held at other times. In Ethiopia's Timkat festival, a tabot (a replica of the tablets of the Ark of the Covenant) is carried in procession to a body of water; in the Byzantine Divine Liturgy, heated water called zeon is added to the communion wine.

**Tashlikh, geshem, and Miriam's cup**
Jewish water traditions. In tashlikh, performed around Rosh Hashanah, bread crumbs symbolizing sins are cast into flowing water; the prayer for rain (geshem) is recited on Shemini Atzeret; and in a modern Passover custom, a cup of water is set out for Miriam alongside Elijah's cup of wine.
